title: Erdős #396 OQ-04 → OQ-01 → OQ-01 → OQ-02 → OQ-02 → OQ-01 → OQ-01: The Wallis Integral Representation of the Central Binomial Coefficient
description: The analytic twin of the parent's combinatorial Wallis product. Where the parent reads the central-binomial recurrence multiplicatively to obtain C(2n,n)/4^n = ∏_{k<n} (2k+1)/(2k+2) in pure rational arithmetic, this entry evaluates the same closed products as definite integrals of powers of sine. Mathlib's Wallis machinery gives ∫₀^π sin²ⁿx dx = π·∏(2k+1)/(2k+2) and ∫₀^π sin²ⁿ⁺¹x dx = 2·∏(2k+2)/(2k+3); composing with the parent's product (and the elementary odd telescope ∏(2k+1)/(2k+3) = 1/(2n+1)) collapses both sides to the headline integral representation ∫₀^π sin²ⁿx dx = π·C(2n,n)/4^n, equivalently C(2n,n) = (4^n/π)·∫₀^π sin²ⁿx dx — a combinatorial number written as an analytic quantity. Multiplying the even and odd integrals cancels the central binomial coefficient entirely, leaving (∫sin²ⁿ)(∫sin²ⁿ⁺¹) = 2π/(2n+1); dividing them exposes the square of the normalised central binomial sequence, (∫sin²ⁿ)/(∫sin²ⁿ⁺¹) = (π/2)(2n+1)(C(2n,n)/4^n)², the object whose 1/√(πn) asymptotic the sibling files certify. No Stirling estimate; the recurrence (via the imported parent) is the only combinatorial input.

overview.historicalContext: The parent entry (Erdős #396 OQ-04 → OQ-01 → OQ-01 → OQ-02 → OQ-02 → OQ-01) exhibits the normalised central binomial coefficient as the Wallis partial product C(2n,n)/4^n = ∏_{k<n} (2k+1)/(2k+2) = (2n−1)!!/(2n)!!, derived entirely from the integer recurrence with no analytic input. Its first open question asked whether this exact double-factorial form can be aligned with Mathlib's Wallis-product development. This file answers that affirmatively from the integral side: the very same closed products are the values of John Wallis' definite integrals of powers of sine, ∫₀^{π} sinⁿx dx, the seventeenth-century computation from which Wallis' product for π originally sprang.
overview.problemStatement: Does the combinatorial Wallis product C(2n,n)/4^n = ∏(2k+1)/(2k+2) admit an analytic integral representation, and what identities does pairing it with the odd-power integral produce?
overview.text: Mathlib evaluates ∫₀^π sin²ⁿx dx = π·∏_{k<n}(2k+1)/(2k+2) and ∫₀^π sin²ⁿ⁺¹x dx = 2·∏_{k<n}(2k+2)/(2k+3). The parent's combinatorial identity rewrites the even product as C(2n,n)/4^n, giving ∫₀^π sin²ⁿx dx = π·C(2n,n)/4^n. For the odd product, the telescope ∏(2k+1)/(2k+3) = 1/(2n+1) together with the even product yields ∏(2k+2)/(2k+3) = 4^n/((2n+1)·C(2n,n)), hence ∫₀^π sin²ⁿ⁺¹x dx = 2·4^n/((2n+1)·C(2n,n)). The product of the two integrals is 2π/(2n+1) (the central binomial coefficient cancels); their quotient is (π/2)(2n+1)(C(2n,n)/4^n)².
overview.proofStrategy: The headline integral_sin_pow_even_eq_centralBinom rewrites Mathlib's integral_sin_pow_even and then the parent's centralBinom_div_eq_wallis_prod (backwards) to identify the product, closing by ring. Inverting with field_simp gives centralBinom_eq_integral. For the odd powers, prod_odd_telescope proves ∏(2k+1)/(2k+3) = 1/(2n+1) by a one-line induction (Finset.prod_range_succ, push_cast, field_simp, ring). wallis_odd_prod_eq then sets A = ∏(2k+1)/(2k+2), B = ∏(2k+2)/(2k+3), observes A·B = ∏(2k+1)/(2k+3) factorwise (Finset.prod_mul_distrib, field_simp), substitutes the parent (A = C/4^n) and the telescope to get A·B·(2n+1) = 1, and clears denominators with eq_div_iff and linear_combination (4^n · (A·B·(2n+1) = 1)). integral_sin_pow_odd_eq_centralBinom is then immediate from integral_sin_pow_odd. The two consequences integral_even_mul_odd_eq and integral_ratio_eq follow by rewriting both integral evaluations and discharging the rational identity with field_simp and ring.
keyInsights: **The Wallis integral is the central binomial coefficient.** ∫₀^π sin²ⁿx dx = π·C(2n,n)/4^n: the same closed product that the parent obtained from the recurrence is the value of Wallis' seventeenth-century integral. The combinatorial and analytic Wallis products are literally equal.

**A combinatorial number written analytically.** Inverting, C(2n,n) = (4^n/π)·∫₀^π sin²ⁿx dx expresses the integer C(2n,n) as a definite integral — the bridge that lets Wallis' analytic limit speak about the integer sequence.

**The odd powers give the reciprocal.** ∫₀^π sin²ⁿ⁺¹x dx = 2·4^n/((2n+1)·C(2n,n)): the (2k+2)/(2k+3) product is the reciprocal central binomial, recovered from the even product and the one-line odd telescope ∏(2k+1)/(2k+3) = 1/(2n+1).

**Multiplying cancels the combinatorics; dividing squares it.** (∫sin²ⁿ)(∫sin²ⁿ⁺¹) = 2π/(2n+1) is free of C(2n,n), while (∫sin²ⁿ)/(∫sin²ⁿ⁺¹) = (π/2)(2n+1)(C(2n,n)/4^n)². The latter is exactly the square of the normalised central binomial sequence — Wallis' theorem (this ratio → 1) is therefore the analytic source of C(2n,n)/4^n ∼ 1/√(πn).
prerequisites: Mathlib's Wallis integral evaluations integral_sin_pow_even and integral_sin_pow_odd over [0, π]
The parent's combinatorial Wallis product C(2n,n)/4^n = ∏_{k<n} (2k+1)/(2k+2) (Erdos396OQ04OQ01OQ01OQ02OQ02OQ01.centralBinom_div_eq_wallis_prod)
Telescoping finite products (Finset.prod_range_succ, Finset.prod_mul_distrib) and field arithmetic (field_simp, eq_div_iff, linear_combination)

conclusion.summary: The combinatorial Wallis product of the parent is identified with John Wallis' definite integral: ∫₀^π sin²ⁿx dx = π·C(2n,n)/4^n, equivalently C(2n,n) = (4^n/π)·∫₀^π sin²ⁿx dx. The odd-power integral is the reciprocal, ∫₀^π sin²ⁿ⁺¹x dx = 2·4^n/((2n+1)·C(2n,n)); their product 2π/(2n+1) is free of the central binomial coefficient, and their quotient (π/2)(2n+1)(C(2n,n)/4^n)² is the square of the normalised central binomial sequence. All 7 theorems are fully machine-checked with no axioms or sorries.
conclusion.implications: This closes the loop between the recurrence-driven combinatorial Wallis product and the classical analytic Wallis integral: they are the same closed product viewed two ways. The quotient identity (π/2)(2n+1)(C(2n,n)/4^n)² is the exact, finite-n statement whose limit (via Mathlib's Real.tendsto_prod_pi_div_two) is Wallis' product π/2, and hence the analytic origin of the central binomial asymptotic C(2n,n) ∼ 4^n/√(πn) pinned in the sibling files. No factorial asymptotics or Stirling estimate are invoked.
openQuestions: Can the quotient identity (∫sin²ⁿ)/(∫sin²ⁿ⁺¹) = (π/2)(2n+1)(C(2n,n)/4^n)² be combined with Mathlib's Wallis-limit Real.tendsto_prod_pi_div_two and the monotonicity ∫sin^{m+1} ≤ ∫sin^m to certify C(2n,n)/4^n ∼ 1/√(πn) purely from the integral squeeze, independently of the Stirling-based route in the sibling capstone?

Does the half-interval refinement ∫₀^{π/2} sin²ⁿx dx = (π/2)·C(2n,n)/4^n (via the sin(π−x) symmetry) yield the Beta-function value B(n+1/2, 1/2) = π·C(2n,n)/4^n, connecting this thread to Mathlib's Gamma/Beta development?

sections.title: Combinatorial vs Analytic Wallis Product
sections.summary: Docstring contrasting the parent's combinatorial product C(2n,n)/4^n = ∏(2k+1)/(2k+2) (pure ℚ-arithmetic of the recurrence) with this file's analytic twin: Mathlib's Wallis integrals ∫₀^π sin²ⁿ = π·∏(2k+1)/(2k+2) and ∫₀^π sin²ⁿ⁺¹ = 2·∏(2k+2)/(2k+3) evaluate the same closed products. Imports Mathlib and the parent, opens Nat/Finset/Real/MeasureTheory/intervalIntegral, opens the namespace.

sections.title: The Odd-Index Telescoping Product
sections.summary: prod_odd_telescope: ∏_{k<n} (2k+1)/(2k+3) = 1/(2n+1), the elementary telescope (1/3)(3/5)(5/7)···((2n−1)/(2n+1)). One-line induction via Finset.prod_range_succ, push_cast, field_simp, ring — the combinatorial input for the odd powers.

sections.title: The Integral Representation of C(2n,n)
sections.summary: integral_sin_pow_even_eq_centralBinom (headline): ∫₀^π sin²ⁿ = π·C(2n,n)/4^n, by rewriting Mathlib's integral_sin_pow_even and the parent's centralBinom_div_eq_wallis_prod backwards, closing by ring. centralBinom_eq_integral inverts it via field_simp: C(2n,n) = (4^n/π)·∫₀^π sin²ⁿ — an integer written as a definite integral.

sections.title: The Odd Powers: the Reciprocal Central Binomial
sections.summary: wallis_odd_prod_eq: ∏(2k+2)/(2k+3) = 4^n/((2n+1)·C(2n,n)), by setting A = ∏(2k+1)/(2k+2), B = ∏(2k+2)/(2k+3), observing A·B = ∏(2k+1)/(2k+3) factorwise (Finset.prod_mul_distrib), substituting A = C/4^n and the telescope to get A·B·(2n+1) = 1, then clearing denominators (eq_div_iff, linear_combination). integral_sin_pow_odd_eq_centralBinom follows: ∫₀^π sin²ⁿ⁺¹ = 2·4^n/((2n+1)·C(2n,n)).

sections.title: Multiplying Cancels, Dividing Squares
sections.summary: integral_even_mul_odd_eq: the product (∫sin²ⁿ)(∫sin²ⁿ⁺¹) = 2π/(2n+1) — the central binomial coefficient cancels completely. integral_ratio_eq: the quotient (∫sin²ⁿ)/(∫sin²ⁿ⁺¹) = (π/2)(2n+1)(C(2n,n)/4^n)² — the square of the normalised central binomial sequence, whose Wallis-limit-to-1 is the analytic origin of C(2n,n)/4^n ∼ 1/√(πn). Both by field_simp after the two integral evaluations.
